description: We are a group of students of different ages and nationalities, sharing an interest in art, space, physics, and programming. We joined this challenge because we are interested in NASA's work and space exploration, and we want to have fun, enjoy our time together, and learn something new.
summary:
Project Summary
We developed Space Mission Design Game, a retro-style engineering simulation in which the player acts as a NASA program manager in 1975. Built in Python with tkinter, it looks like a vintage telemetry terminal and is played entirely by keyboard. The player designs a multi-stage rocket for three missions of rising difficulty: Low Earth Orbit, ISS rendezvous and a lunar mission. They pick real components, such as the F-1 and RS-25 engines and the Crew Dragon, Apollo and Orion spacecraft. They must stay within a budget and a deadline while keeping the trust of a skeptical Flight Director.
The game applies real aerospace physics. It uses the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation for Δv, enforces a thrust-to-weight ratio of at least 1.15, and checks propellant and power compatibility. Launch is interactive, with manual staging and random in-flight anomalies.
It matters because it turns abstract mission design into hands-on decisions. Players see how engineering, science and management constraints conflict, which makes spaceflight engineering accessible and engaging. All game data is stored in an external JSON file, so new parts and missions are easy to add.
details:
SPACE MISSION DESIGN GAME

Project Overview, Architectural Breakdown, and Technical Master Document

1. The Concept: A 1975 NASA Telemetry Terminal

At its core, Space Mission Design Game is an atmospheric, role-playing engineering simulation that places you directly behind the glowing monochrome screen of an imaginary NASA employee working during the golden era of space exploration (circa 1975).

Rather than presenting itself as a modern, glossy video game, the project is meticulously designed to feel like a repurposed vintage mainframe computer terminal operating inside the Kennedy Space Center. Every design choice—from the stark, high-contrast text layout and monospace typography (Courier New) to the total absence of mouse controls and the reliance purely on keyboard inputs—is intentionally crafted to make you feel like an actual aerospace program manager sitting in a dimly lit control room, racing against a ticking calendar.

The Burden of Responsibility and Corporate Bureaucracy

You aren't just playing a game; you are stepping into the heavy shoes of a bureaucrat-engineer tasked with making high-stakes, real-world compromises. The concept revolves around constant friction between four distinct departments:

The Engineer: Brawling for raw power, multi-stage heavy rockets, and massive fuel tanks.

The Scientist: Demanding heavy payloads, advanced life-support systems, and complex sensor arrays.

The Avionics Specialist: Worrying about guidance computers, power generation, and precision telemetry.

The Manager (You): Forced to balance all of these competing demands against a strict government budget, tight deadlines, and a skeptical, relentless Flight Director (the "Boss").

Random emergency events—such as unexpected congressional budget cuts, solar storms, or failing fuel valves—amplify the feeling that you are managing a living, breathing, chaotic space program where things constantly go wrong. The thematic journey culminates in a striking psychological transition: moving from cold, quiet columns of numbers in an office to the roaring, smoke-filled chaos of the launch pad (Launch Pad 39A).

2. Architectural Overview & Design Philosophy

Tech Stack & UI Framework

Built purely in Python using the standard tkinter library, the application features a fixed-dimension interface (1120780 pixels) styled as an austere 1975 NASA computer terminal. The UI utilizes monospaced fonts, stark high-contrast color palettes (pure black backgrounds with white, green, and red text), and custom-rendered dynamic borders to evoke a retro-futuristic telemetry console.

Data-Driven Decoupling via JSON

Game configuration data—including difficulty brackets, propulsion engines, propellant tanks, spacecraft hulls, life support systems, and scientific instruments—is completely externalized into an external configuration file (game_data.json). This structural separation allows easy modification or expansion of aerospace parts without ever touching core application logic.

Custom Visual Assets

To complete the authentic retro atmosphere, all graphical illustrations and component art displayed within the terminal interface have been custom-created by us, pairing perfectly with the vintage aesthetic.

Multithreading for Audio & TTS

To prevent GUI freezing during intensive background operations, the script leverages Python’s threading module. It runs asynchronous threads for text-to-speech voice synthesis (pyttsx3) and procedural WAV file generation.

3. Core Gameplay Mechanics & State Machine

The game operates through a deterministic finite state machine controlled by specific key bindings across several screens (TITLE, LEVEL_SELECT, BRIEFING, HUB, ASSEMBLY, LOADING_ASSEMBLY, COUNTDOWN, FLIGHT_SIM, FLIGHT, EVALUATION, FIRED_EVENT). Mouse interactions are intentionally disabled to reinforce the old-school terminal aesthetic.

Resource Management Loop

Budget & Time Windows: Players must balance finite monetary funds ($M) against a ticking calendar limit. Every action—whether purchasing heavy-duty cryogenic tanks or hiring specialized technicians—consumes both capital and preparation days.

Boss Trust Metric: Management trust starts at 80%. Missing deadlines, exceeding budgets, or failing high-stakes 50/50 administrative gambles drops trust. If trust hits 0%, a terminal failure event triggers ("YOU ARE FIRED!").

Aerospace Engineering & Physics Equations

Tsiolkovsky Rocket Equation: The script calculates stage-by-stage and cumulative velocity changes using the classic Tsiolkovsky equation across a three-stage architecture:

v=Ispgmstartmend

Thrust-to-Weight Ratio (TWR): Evaluates total vehicle mass against maximum sea-level thrust, enforcing a hard safety floor (TWR1.15) to prevent launchpad structural crashes.

Compatibility Matrix: Dynamically checks chemical compatibility between engines and fuel tanks (e.g., matching Kerolox, Methalox, or Hydrolox propellants) and verifies that life support systems and electrical generation match crew requirements.

4. Advanced Multimedia & Audio Subsystems

One of the most technically intricate aspects of the script is its native procedural audio and speech synthesis framework:

Text-to-Speech (TTS) Director Module: Uses pyttsx3 to voice-act dynamic dialogue from the "Flight Director/Boss" during briefings, warnings, and random crisis events, running asynchronously to avoid locking the main GUI event loop.

Procedural Rocket Engine Sound Synthesizer (play_engine_roar):

If a custom .wav file is absent, the script dynamically generates a temporary raw audio stream using Python's built-in wave and struct modules.

It synthesizes brown noise (passing white noise through a low-pass filter) blended with deep sub-bass acoustic vibrations (32Hz and 58Hz oscillators) coupled with an amplitude envelope to simulate a massive Saturn V-class rocket roar.

Procedural Explosion Generator (play_explosion_sound):

Constructs an instantaneous acoustic shockwave by combining fast-decaying exponential envelopes, a downward-sweeping sub-bass frequency thump (90Hz to 28Hz), and random high-frequency crackling to simulate high-energy turbopump ignition.

5. Interactive Flight Simulation Loop

The climax of the game transitions from a strategic builder into an active reflex and decision-making challenge:

Manual Staging Overwrite (FLIGHT_SIM): During powered ascent, a multi-stage propellant timer counts down. Players must watch fuel depletion and hit the Spacebar precisely at 0.0s to execute explosive bolt separation. Perfect timing yields clean staging, whereas mistiming introduces Delta-V penalties.

Stochastic Flight Events & Anomalies (FLIGHT): Mid-flight and orbital insertion phases trigger procedural hazards (e.g., Max-Q structural vibrations, solar storms, space debris fields, or fuel manifold micro-fractures). Players must use directional inputs to choose mitigation strategies that trade off Delta-V reserves, science points, and structural failure probabilities.

6. Comprehensive Catalog of Implemented Aerospace Components (game_data.json)

The technical foundation of the game relies on an exhaustive dataset structured within game_data.json:

A. Mission Difficulty Brackets

Level 1: Low Earth Orbit (LEO)

Target: Earth Orbit

Budget: $420M | Time: 110days | Staff: 30 personnel

Requirements: v100m/s | Science: 40pts

Level 2: ISS Rendezvous

Target: International Space Station (408km)

Budget: $600M | Time: 140days | Staff: 40 personnel

Requirements: v155m/s | Science: 85pts

Level 3: Lunar Mission (Moon)

Target: Lunar Orbit & Surface

Budget: $850M | Time: 180days | Staff: 50 personnel

Requirements: v230m/s | Science: 140pts

B. Propulsion Systems & Tanks (Stages 1, 2, and 3)

Stage 1 Engines: Features historical and modern heavy-lift plants such as the Rocketdyne F-1 (7,740.5kN, $\text{I}{sp}$ 304s, LOX/RP-1), RS-68 (3,312kN, $\text{I}{sp}$ 420s, LOX/LH2), RS-25 (2,278.8kN, Isp 452.3s), Merlin 1C (480kN), Raptor 3 (2,697kN, Methalox), RD-180 (4,152kN), and Vulcain 2 (1,350kN).

Stage 1 Tanks: Includes heavy structural and cryogenic vessels like the S-IC (Saturn V booster), Falcon 9 v1.2, SLS Core Stage, EPC (Ariane 5), Glenn Stage 1, and Super Heavy.

Upper Stages (Stages 2 & 3): Incorporates high-efficiency engines and upper-stage tanks such as the RD-0124, Vinci, Merlin 1D Vacuum, Rockerdyne J-2, paired with advanced tanks like the S-II, S-IVB, and Sojuz Blok-I.

C. Spacecraft Payloads

Crew Dragon (SpaceX): Mass 7.7t, habitable volume 9.3m3, trunk volume 37m3, integrated solar trunk (5kW generation), capacity up to 4 crew members.

Apollo Command Module: Mass 11.9t, volume 8.95m3, hydrogen fuel cell power source (2kW consumption, 3kW generation), capacity for 3 crew members.

Orion (Lockheed Martin / ESA): Mass 15.483t, volume 19.5m3, deployable European Service Module solar arrays (11kW generation), deep-space radiation shielding, capacity for 4 crew members.

D. Life Support, Science, and Power Systems

ECLSS: Open LiOH System utilizing lithium hydroxide canisters for CO2 scrubbing, supporting up to 4 crew members.

Scientific Instruments: Real-world calibrated instrument packages including the Cosmic Ray Isotope Spectrometer (CRIS) (Caltech/NASA), Magnetometer (MAG) (Goddard/Imperial College), High-Energy Particle Detector (HEPD-02), Cosmic Dust Analyzer (CDA) (Max Planck Institute), and the Kairospace 250mm Camera.

Power Systems: Advanced RTG Generator (Lockheed Aerospace) providing long-duration radioisotope thermoelectric generation (8.5kW) independent of solar exposure.
